As this translation isn't very good atm[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 08:22, 13 March 2025 (UTC)}} [[File:Three Palace Sanctuaries.jpg|thumb|Three Palace Sanctuaries]] The {{Nihongo|'''Three Palace Sanctuaries'''|宮中三殿|Kyūchū sanden}} are a group of structures in the precincts of the [[Tokyo Imperial Palace]] in [[:en:Japan|Japan]]. They are used in imperial religious ceremonies, including weddings and [[Enthronement of the Japanese emperor|enthronements]]. The three sanctuaries are: * ''Kashiko-dokoro'' (賢所) – the central shrine, enshrining a replica of the mirror [[Yata no Kagami]], representing the mythological ancestress of the [[:en:Imperial Family of Japan|Imperial Family]], [[Amaterasu]]. (For the enthronements in [[:en:Kyoto|Kyoto]] of [[:en:Emperor Taishō|Emperor Taishō]] in 1915 and of [[:en:Emperor Shōwa|Emperor Shōwa]] in 1928, the mirror was transported by special [[:en:Rolling stock|Rolling stock]] known as the ''Kashiko-dokoro Jōgyosha'' (賢所乗御車) from the name of this sanctuary.) The ''[[:en:Yasakani no magatama|Yasakani no magatama]]'' or Sacred Jewel, one of the [[:en:Imperial Regalia of Japan|Imperial Regalia of Japan]], is also said to be housed in the Kashiko-dokoro. * ''Kōrei-den'' (皇霊殿) – the [[:en:Ancestral spirits|Ancestral Spirits]] Sanctuary, enshrining the departed spirits of the Imperial Family from one year after their death. * ''Shin-den'' (神殿) – the Sanctuary of the ''[[Kami]]'', enshrining the ''[[Amatsukami]]'' (天津神) from [[Takamagahara]] and the ''Kunitsukami'' (国津神) from [[Japanese mythology]]. {{infobox Shinto shrine | name = Kyūchū Sanden | image = [[File:Three Palace Sanctuaries.jpg|290px]] | location = {{JPN}}・[[:en:Tokyo|Tokyo Metropolis]]・[[:en:Chiyoda, Tokyo|Chiyoda Ward]]・[[:en:Chiyoda, Chiyoda, Tokyo|Chiyoda]] 1-1 | coordinates = {{coord|35|40|54|N|139|44|59|E|display=inline,title}} | enshrined deities = Ken-sho: {{ill|Amaterasu Ōmikami|ja|天照大御神|1=Amaterasu|lt=Amaterasu Ōmikami|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amaterasu Ōmikami|13=User:Immanuelle/Amaterasu|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 天照大神}}
Kōrei-den: [[:en:List of emperors of Japan|Emperors]]・{{ill|Imperial Family|ja|皇族|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imperial Family|qq=|1=Imperial Family of Japan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11581068}} spirits
Shin-den: {{ill|Tenshin Chigi|ja|天神地祇|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tenshin Chigi|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 天津神・国津神|1=Amatsukami and Kunitsukami|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11442793}} | shrine Rank = None | annual festival = Ken-sho: January 3 ({{ill|Ganshiki-sai|ja|元始祭|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ganshiki-sai|qq=|1=Genshisai|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11387821}}) ・ October 17 ([[:en:Kannamesai Festival|Kannamesai]])
Kōrei-den: January 7 ({{ill|Senteisai|ja|先帝祭|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Senteisai|qq=|1=Previous Emperor Festival|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11388139}}) ・ {{ill|Vernal Equinox Day|ja|春分日|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Vernal Equinox Day|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 春分|1=Chunfen|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1339268}} ({{ill|Spring Imperial Festival|ja|春季皇霊祭|1=Kōreisai|lt=Spring Kōreisai|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Spring Imperial Festival|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōreisai|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 皇霊祭}}) ・ April 3 ({{ill|Jimmu Tennō-sai|ja|神武天皇祭|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Jimmu Tennō-sai|qq=|1=Emperor Jinmu Festival|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11590440}}) ・ {{ill|Autumnal Equinox Day|ja|秋分日|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Autumnal Equinox Day|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 秋分|1=Qiufen|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1200436}} (Autumn Imperial Festival)
Shin-den: Vernal Equinox Day (Spring Shrine Festival) ・ Autumnal Equinox Day (Autumn Shrine Festival)
Shinka-den: November 23 ([[:en:Niiname-no-Matsuri|Niinamesai]]) }} '''Kyūchū Sanden''' (宮中三殿【きゅうちゅうさんでん】) is the collective name for the three sanctuaries—the '''Ken-sho''' (賢所), '''Kōrei-den''' (皇霊殿), and '''Shin-den''' (神殿)—located within the [[:en:Tokyo Imperial Palace|Imperial Palace]]’s {{ill|Fukiage Gyoen|ja|吹上御苑|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Fukiage Gyoen|qq=|1=Fukiage Gyoen|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11288366}}. These three halls are also collectively referred to as the “Ken-sho” (賢所, けんしょ).{{Cite book|和書|title=Imperial Household Encyclopedia (Reiwa Edition)|date=2019th year 11月30日|year=2019|publisher={{ill|KADOKAWA|ja|株式会社KADOKAWA|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/KADOKAWA|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to KADOKAWA|1=Kadokawa Corporation|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q17224985}}}} Kyūchū Sanden consists of three parts: at its center is the Ken-sho, which enshrines the imperial ancestral deity {{ill|Amaterasu Ōmikami|ja|天照大御神|1=Amaterasu|lt=Amaterasu Ōmikami|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amaterasu Ōmikami|13=User:Immanuelle/Amaterasu|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 天照大神}}; to its west is the Kōrei-den, which enshrines the spirits of successive emperors {{ill|List of Emperors|ja|歴代の天皇|lt=Emperors|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/List of Emperors|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 天皇の一覧|1=list of Emperors of Japan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q188210}} and empresses as well as other members of the {{ill|Imperial Family|ja|皇族|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imperial Family|qq=|1=Imperial Family of Japan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11581068}}; and to its east is the Shin-den, which enshrines the myriad kami ({{ill|Tenshin Chigi|ja|天神地祇|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tenshin Chigi|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 天津神・国津神|1=Amatsukami and Kunitsukami|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11442793}}) of the Japanese pantheon.{{Sfn|皇室75号|2017|p=43}} == Overview == {{Double image aside|right|Emperor Akihito 199011 1.jpg|290|Emperor Akihito, Daijosai (1990).jpg|172|{{ill|Kōroshūzome Gohō|ja|黄櫨染御袍|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōroshūzome Gohō|qq=|1=Kōrozen no gohō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11677782}} and ceremonial garments worn during the reign of [[:en:Akihito|Akihito]]}} Kyūchū Sanden is constructed facing south, with the Ken-sho centrally located, the Kōrei-den to its west, and the Shin-den to its east.{{Sfn|皇室75号|2017|p=42}} The Ken-sho is the largest among the three. The architecture of Kyūchū Sanden is of a single-story [[:en:East Asian hip-and-gable roof|Irimoya-zukuri]] style with {{ill|Saimoto|ja|妻入|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Saimoto|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 切妻造|1=rake-overhanging gabled roof|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q13308575}}, built of white wood with decorative elements on the front and back.{{Sfn|皇室75号|2017|p=42}} Originally, the roofs were clad in {{ill|Hinoki bark|ja|檜皮葺|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hinoki bark|qq=|1=cypress bark roof|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q90373477}}, but were later replaced with copper plates.{{Cite book|title=Shirarezaru Kōshitsu – From Traditional Ceremonies to the Work of the Imperial Household Agency|date=2010th year 1月30日|year=2010|publisher=[[:en:Kawade Shobō Shinsha|Kawade Shobo Shinsha]]}} The interiors of the three halls are divided into the outer court, inner court, and innermost court (naichinai-den).{{Sfn|皇室75号|2017|p=42}} The buildings feature wooden floors, with sliding doors such as half-fusuma (【半蔀】, hajitomi) and shōji, and are surrounded by lattice work ({{ill|Sudare|ja|簀子|lt=Sudare|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sudare|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to すのこ|1=duckboards|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q2933208}}). In front, each has wooden steps, further preceded by stone steps.{{Sfn|皇室75号|2017|p=42}} == Rituals and Ceremonies == {{seealso|Ritual ceremonies of the Imperial Palace}} Within Kyūchū Sanden, in order to oversee the imperial rituals, a separate internal organization distinct from the state administrative body of the [[:en:Imperial Household Agency|Imperial Household Agency]] is established, known as the '''Chōten-shoku''' (掌典職).{{Cite news |title=宮中祭祀|newspaper= |date= |author=宮内庁|url=https://www.kunaicho.go.jp/about/gokomu/kyuchu/saishi/saishi.html|accessdate=2014-10-02}} Under the head of the Chōten, subordinate positions including the Chōten-chō, Chōten, and Naichōten are appointed.{{Sfn|皇室75号|2017|p=43}} The Naichōten (unmarried women serving a role equivalent to miko at ordinary shrines) all reside in the north side of the compound. Every morning from 8:00 AM, the Naichōten in the Ken-sho and Kōrei-den, and the Chōten in the Shin-den, perform the “Nikku no Gi” by offering {{ill|sake|ja|清酒|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/sake|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 日本酒}} and sacred food ([[:en:Shinsen|Shinsen]]). At 8:30 AM, the on-duty chamberlain of the [[:en:Board of Chamberlains|Imperial Household Agency Attendant Office]] conducts the “Maichō Godaihai” on behalf of the emperor in all three halls. These rituals, Nikku no Gi and Maichō Godaihai, are carried out without fail even during periods when the emperor is not in residence ({{ill|Haichō|ja|廃朝|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Haichō|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}) or during periods of imperial mourning. The ceremonial practices of Kyūchū Sanden were established after the Meiji Restoration, through successive reforms and gradual consolidation of imperial rites, and are understood to have been finalized on April 2 (lunar calendar) in the 5th year of Meiji ([[:en:1872|1872]] / May 8) shortly after the establishment of the Ministry of Divinities ([[:en:Ministry of Religion (Japan)|Ministry of Religion]]).{{Cite news |title=維新期「宮中三殿」成立史の一考察―毎朝御拝「石灰壇」祭祀の終焉として―|newspaper=明治聖徳記念学会紀要〔復刊第45号〕|date=2008-11|author=石野浩司|url=http://www.mkc.gr.jp/seitoku/pdf/f45-4.pdf|accessdate=2014-10-02}} At that time, the sandai-den (砂拝殿) within the Imperial Palace was relocated to the Akasaka Temporary Imperial Palace after being damaged by a fire in September of [[:en:1873|1873]] (Meiji 6). The current structures of Kyūchū Sanden were designed by {{ill|Kikosei Kiyokage|ja|木子清敬|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kikosei Kiyokage|qq=|1=Kigo Kiyoyoshi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11518290}}, a first-class craftsman of the former [[:en:Ministry of the Imperial Household|Ministry of the Imperial Household]], completed in October [[:en:1888|1888]] (Meiji 21) and relocated on January 9 [[:en:1889|1889]] (Meiji 22). During World War II in [[:en:1944|1944]] (Showa 19), the structures were temporarily relocated to the Imperial Palace’s air-raid shelter (the Osai-ko, 御斎庫) to avoid air raids, returning after the end of the war in [[:en:1945|1945]] (Showa 20), and in [[:en:2004|2004]] (Heisei 16) on June 18 were once temporarily moved to a provisional hall (the Kari-dono, 仮殿) set several dozen meters away for seismic deterioration inspections (returning on the 27th of the same month). Additionally, several ancillary buildings are located within the compound. To the west is the Shinka-den (神嘉殿), normally an empty hall, but on November 30 each year, the [[:en:Niiname-no-Matsuri|Niinamesai]] is held and on New Year’s Day ({{ill|Gantan|ja|元旦|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gantan|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 元日|1=New Year's Day|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q196627}}) the 【Shihōhai】 is performed in its front garden. Other structures include the Ryōki-den (綾綺殿), where ceremonies such as the ritual changing of attire for the emperor and empress take place; the Tōgū-bin-den (東宮便殿), where the Crown Prince and Crown Princess change attire; the Kagurasha (神楽舎), where kagura is offered; the Sōgakusha (奏楽舎), where gagaku is performed by musicians; the Hidari-akusha (左幄舎) and Migi-akusha (右幄舎), where attendants wait; the Ken-sho main gate (賢所正門) facing the Ken-sho; and the Shinka-mon (新嘉門) facing the Shinka-den. == The Three Halls == === Kashiko-dokoro === {{main|Kashiko-dokoro}} [[File:Yata no Kagami, artist impression.png|thumb|Yata no Kagami (image); actual object is not publicly displayed]] The Ken-sho enshrines the sacred mirror ([[:en:Yata no Kagami|Yata no Kagami]]) and venerates the ancestral deity {{ill|Amaterasu Ōmikami|ja|天照大御神|1=Amaterasu|lt=Amaterasu Ōmikami|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amaterasu Ōmikami|13=User:Immanuelle/Amaterasu|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 天照大神}}.{{Sfn|皇室75号|2017|p=43}} During the Heian period, the Ken-sho was located at the {{ill|Unmei-den|ja|温明殿|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Unmei-den|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, and from the Kamakura period (and subsequently during the Muromachi period) it was situated at the {{ill|Shunkō-den|ja|春興殿|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shunkō-den|qq=|1=Shunkōden|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11513798}}; in earlier times, it was managed by the {{ill|Naishi|ja|内侍|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Naishi|qq=|1=naishi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11393857}}, hence it was also called the “Naishidokoro” (内侍所).{{Cite web|和書|url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E8%B3%A2%E6%89%80-44278|title=賢所|accessdate=2021-01-17|publisher=[[:en:Kotobank|Kotobank]]}} The Chōten and Naichōten serve the sacred functions, protecting the “sacred fire” (which signifies a holy flame) and are subject to strict protocols such as the “Jisei” system to avoid defilement. Ancient imperial rituals ([[:en:Ritual ceremonies of the Imperial Palace|Ceremonies of the Japanese Imperial Palace]]) have long been performed here, and it is at this location that marriage ceremonies ({{ill|Kekkon no Gi|ja|結婚の儀|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kekkon no Gi|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 皇室の儀式|1=Japanese Imperial Rituals|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11581030}}) welcoming former Empress Dowager [[:en:Empress Michiko|Michiko†Jōkōgō_Michiko]], Empress [[:en:Empress Masako|Masako†Kōgō_Masako]], and other imperial consorts have been held. In such ceremonies, when the empress exits the Ken-sho, the marriage is considered to be solemnized. === Kōrei-den === The Kōrei-den enshrines the spirits of successive emperors and other members of the {{ill|Imperial Family|ja|皇族|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imperial Family|qq=|1=Imperial Family of Japan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11581068}}.{{Sfn|皇室75号|2017|p=43}} During the Meiji Restoration, under the Shinbutsu Hanzenrei, reforms in imperial rites were implemented. In 1862 (Meiji 2), the re-established [[:en:Department of Divinities|Department of Divinities]] (later the Ministry of Divinities) built an auxiliary hall and enshrined the spirits of successive emperors in the Shinto style. As a result, the “Kurodo” (黒戸)—which had been used to enshrine emperors in the Buddhist style since the Heian period—was abolished, and the imperial tablets and statues were transferred to {{ill|Reimei-den at Sensō-ji|ja|霊明殿|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Reimei-den at Sensō-ji|qq=|1=Reimeiden|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q109357129}} at [[:en:Sennyū-ji|Senyū-ji]].{{Cite journal|author=石野浩司|year=2015|title=Establishment of “Reimei-den” during the Meiji Period at Senyū-ji—Imperial Rites and Its Connection with Senyū-ji|journal=明治聖徳記念学会起要|volume=復刊第52号|page=}} On September 14, 1871 (Meiji 4), the Ken-sho was relocated within the palace.{{Sfn|皇典講究所|1909|p=18}} After the relocation to the Akasaka Temporary Imperial Palace in 1873 (Meiji 6) due to fire damage, in 1877 (Meiji 10) the spirits of empresses and other imperial family members were enshrined together with those of the emperors.{{Sfn|皇典講究所|1909|p=18}} In 1885 (Meiji 18), even those emperors who had been posthumously awarded a 【尊号】 were also enshrined.{{Sfn|皇典講究所|1909|p=18}} In 1889 (Meiji 22), with the reconstruction of the Imperial Palace, a new building was constructed on the west side of the Ken-sho.{{Sfn|皇典講究所|1909|p=18}} It is customary that the spirits of the emperor and imperial family are enshrined in the Kōrei-den one year after their death.{{Cite web|和書|url=https://www.nikkei.com/article/DGXNZO56020230Q3A610C1CR0000/|title=天皇陛下、寛仁さまの墓所を参拝|accessdate=2013-06-10|publisher=[[:en:The Nikkei|Nikkei]]}} Every year, the Spring Imperial Festival is held on the Vernal Equinox Day and the Autumn Imperial Festival on the Autumnal Equinox Day. Additionally, on January 7 the Shōwa Tennō-sai (Senteisai) is held, and on April 3 the Jimmu Tennō-sai takes place; in certain ceremonial years, the emperor’s memorial rites are conducted at the imperial mausoleum, and the Crown Prince and Crown Princess participate in rites at the Kōrei-den. === Shin-den === It enshrines the eight million kami, namely {{ill|Tenshin and Kunitsugami|ja|天津神・国津神|1=Kami#Amatsukami_and_Kunitsukami|2=ja|3=天津神・国津神|4=zh|5=天津神與國津神|6=ko|7=아마쓰카미·구니쓰카미|lt=Amatsukami and Kunitsukami|lt=Tenshin Chigi|lt_ja=天神地祇|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tenshin and Kunitsugami|qq=|comment=enwiki is a redirect}}, who comprise the myriad deities of Japan. {{Sfn|皇室75号|2017|p=43}} Originally, this facility was dedicated to enshrining the eight gods and was known as {{ill|Yatsugamaden|ja|八神殿|1=Hasshinden|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yatsugamaden|13=User:Immanuelle/Hasshinden|qq=}}. From the medieval period onward it was maintained in the western wing of the [[:en:Department of Divinities|Department of Divinities]], but by the time of [[:en:Emperor Ōgimachi|Emperor Shōchin-machi]], the associated government offices had been lost. {{Sfn|皇典講究所|1909|p=24}} Consequently, the Urabe clan performed ritual offerings at Kaguragaoka in Yoshida Village, Kyoto, establishing it as a sacred site. However, in Tenshō 18 (1590), by imperial authorization, it was designated as acting on behalf of the Jingi-kan, and the sacred object of the eight gods was enshrined within the residence of the {{ill|Hakugawa Hakuō Family|ja|白川伯王家|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hakugawa Hakuō Family|qq=|1=Shirakawa clan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11579697}}. {{Sfn|皇典講究所|1909|p=25}} In the Meiji era, the [[:en:Department of Divinities|Department of Divinities]] constructed a shrine in Tokyo, and the sacred object was enshrined there on December 17, Meiji 2 (1862). {{Sfn|皇典講究所|1909|p=25-26}} After the Jingi-kan was reorganized into the Ministry of Divinities—and that ministry was abolished in Meiji 5 (1872)—the eight gods and {{ill|Tenshin Chigi|ja|天神地祇|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tenshin Chigi|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 天津神・国津神|1=Amatsukami and Kunitsukami|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11442793}} were transferred to the Imperial Court. On November 27 of that same year they were enshrined together and the shrine was renamed as the Shin-den. {{Sfn|皇典講究所|1909|p=26-27}} Every year, on the Vernal Equinox Day and the Autumnal Equinox Day, the spring and autumn Shin-den festivals are held. == Footnotes == {{Reflist}} == References == * {{Citation|和書|author=皇典講究所|title=宮中三殿並に祝祭日解説|publisher=国晃館|year=1909}} * As this translation isn't very good atm[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 08:22, 13 March 2025 (UTC)}} [[File:Three Palace Sanctuaries.jpg|thumb|Three Palace Sanctuaries]] The {{Nihongo|'''Three Palace Sanctuaries'''|宮中三殿|Kyūchū sanden}} are a group of structures in the precincts of the [[Tokyo Imperial Palace]] in [[:en:Japan|Japan]]. They are used in imperial religious ceremonies, including weddings and [[Enthronement of the Japanese emperor|enthronements]]. The three sanctuaries are: * ''Kashiko-dokoro'' (賢所) – the central shrine, enshrining a replica of the mirror [[Yata no Kagami]], representing the mythological ancestress of the [[:en:Imperial Family of Japan|Imperial Family]], [[Amaterasu]]. (For the enthronements in [[:en:Kyoto|Kyoto]] of [[:en:Emperor Taishō|Emperor Taishō]] in 1915 and of [[:en:Emperor Shōwa|Emperor Shōwa]] in 1928, the mirror was transported by special [[:en:Rolling stock|Rolling stock]] known as the ''Kashiko-dokoro Jōgyosha'' (賢所乗御車) from the name of this sanctuary.) The ''[[:en:Yasakani no magatama|Yasakani no magatama]]'' or Sacred Jewel, one of the [[:en:Imperial Regalia of Japan|Imperial Regalia of Japan]], is also said to be housed in the Kashiko-dokoro. * ''Kōrei-den'' (皇霊殿) – the [[:en:Ancestral spirits|Ancestral Spirits]] Sanctuary, enshrining the departed spirits of the Imperial Family from one year after their death. * ''Shin-den'' (神殿) – the Sanctuary of the ''[[Kami]]'', enshrining the ''[[Amatsukami]]'' (天津神) from [[Takamagahara]] and the ''Kunitsukami'' (国津神) from [[Japanese mythology]]. {{infobox Shinto shrine | name = Kyūchū Sanden | image = [[File:Three Palace Sanctuaries.jpg|290px]] | location = {{JPN}}・[[:en:Tokyo|Tokyo Metropolis]]・[[:en:Chiyoda, Tokyo|Chiyoda Ward]]・[[:en:Chiyoda, Chiyoda, Tokyo|Chiyoda]] 1-1 | coordinates = {{coord|35|40|54|N|139|44|59|E|display=inline,title}} | enshrined deities = Ken-sho: {{ill|Amaterasu Ōmikami|ja|天照大御神|1=Amaterasu|lt=Amaterasu Ōmikami|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amaterasu Ōmikami|13=User:Immanuelle/Amaterasu|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 天照大神}}
Kōrei-den: [[:en:List of emperors of Japan|Emperors]]・{{ill|Imperial Family|ja|皇族|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imperial Family|qq=|1=Imperial Family of Japan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11581068}} spirits
Shin-den: {{ill|Tenshin Chigi|ja|天神地祇|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tenshin Chigi|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 天津神・国津神|1=Amatsukami and Kunitsukami|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11442793}} | shrine Rank = None | annual festival = Ken-sho: January 3 ({{ill|Ganshiki-sai|ja|元始祭|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ganshiki-sai|qq=|1=Genshisai|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11387821}}) ・ October 17 ([[:en:Kannamesai Festival|Kannamesai]])
Kōrei-den: January 7 ({{ill|Senteisai|ja|先帝祭|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Senteisai|qq=|1=Previous Emperor Festival|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11388139}}) ・ {{ill|Vernal Equinox Day|ja|春分日|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Vernal Equinox Day|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 春分|1=Chunfen|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1339268}} ({{ill|Spring Imperial Festival|ja|春季皇霊祭|1=Kōreisai|lt=Spring Kōreisai|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Spring Imperial Festival|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōreisai|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 皇霊祭}}) ・ April 3 ({{ill|Jimmu Tennō-sai|ja|神武天皇祭|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Jimmu Tennō-sai|qq=|1=Emperor Jinmu Festival|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11590440}}) ・ {{ill|Autumnal Equinox Day|ja|秋分日|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Autumnal Equinox Day|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 秋分|1=Qiufen|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1200436}} (Autumn Imperial Festival)
Shin-den: Vernal Equinox Day (Spring Shrine Festival) ・ Autumnal Equinox Day (Autumn Shrine Festival)
Shinka-den: November 23 ([[:en:Niiname-no-Matsuri|Niinamesai]]) }} '''Kyūchū Sanden''' (宮中三殿【きゅうちゅうさんでん】) is the collective name for the three sanctuaries—the '''Ken-sho''' (賢所), '''Kōrei-den''' (皇霊殿), and '''Shin-den''' (神殿)—located within the [[:en:Tokyo Imperial Palace|Imperial Palace]]’s {{ill|Fukiage Gyoen|ja|吹上御苑|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Fukiage Gyoen|qq=|1=Fukiage Gyoen|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11288366}}. These three halls are also collectively referred to as the “Ken-sho” (賢所, けんしょ).{{Cite book|和書|title=Imperial Household Encyclopedia (Reiwa Edition)|date=2019th year 11月30日|year=2019|publisher={{ill|KADOKAWA|ja|株式会社KADOKAWA|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/KADOKAWA|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to KADOKAWA|1=Kadokawa Corporation|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q17224985}}}} Kyūchū Sanden consists of three parts: at its center is the Ken-sho, which enshrines the imperial ancestral deity {{ill|Amaterasu Ōmikami|ja|天照大御神|1=Amaterasu|lt=Amaterasu Ōmikami|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amaterasu Ōmikami|13=User:Immanuelle/Amaterasu|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 天照大神}}; to its west is the Kōrei-den, which enshrines the spirits of successive emperors {{ill|List of Emperors|ja|歴代の天皇|lt=Emperors|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/List of Emperors|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 天皇の一覧|1=list of Emperors of Japan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q188210}} and empresses as well as other members of the {{ill|Imperial Family|ja|皇族|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imperial Family|qq=|1=Imperial Family of Japan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11581068}}; and to its east is the Shin-den, which enshrines the myriad kami ({{ill|Tenshin Chigi|ja|天神地祇|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tenshin Chigi|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 天津神・国津神|1=Amatsukami and Kunitsukami|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11442793}}) of the Japanese pantheon.{{Sfn|皇室75号|2017|p=43}} == Overview == {{Double image aside|right|Emperor Akihito 199011 1.jpg|290|Emperor Akihito, Daijosai (1990).jpg|172|{{ill|Kōroshūzome Gohō|ja|黄櫨染御袍|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōroshūzome Gohō|qq=|1=Kōrozen no gohō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11677782}} and ceremonial garments worn during the reign of [[:en:Akihito|Akihito]]}} Kyūchū Sanden is constructed facing south, with the Ken-sho centrally located, the Kōrei-den to its west, and the Shin-den to its east.{{Sfn|皇室75号|2017|p=42}} The Ken-sho is the largest among the three. The architecture of Kyūchū Sanden is of a single-story [[:en:East Asian hip-and-gable roof|Irimoya-zukuri]] style with {{ill|Saimoto|ja|妻入|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Saimoto|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 切妻造|1=rake-overhanging gabled roof|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q13308575}}, built of white wood with decorative elements on the front and back.{{Sfn|皇室75号|2017|p=42}} Originally, the roofs were clad in {{ill|Hinoki bark|ja|檜皮葺|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hinoki bark|qq=|1=cypress bark roof|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q90373477}}, but were later replaced with copper plates.{{Cite book|title=Shirarezaru Kōshitsu – From Traditional Ceremonies to the Work of the Imperial Household Agency|date=2010th year 1月30日|year=2010|publisher=[[:en:Kawade Shobō Shinsha|Kawade Shobo Shinsha]]}} The interiors of the three halls are divided into the outer court, inner court, and innermost court (naichinai-den).{{Sfn|皇室75号|2017|p=42}} The buildings feature wooden floors, with sliding doors such as half-fusuma (【半蔀】, hajitomi) and shōji, and are surrounded by lattice work ({{ill|Sudare|ja|簀子|lt=Sudare|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sudare|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to すのこ|1=duckboards|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q2933208}}). In front, each has wooden steps, further preceded by stone steps.{{Sfn|皇室75号|2017|p=42}} == Rituals and Ceremonies == {{seealso|Ritual ceremonies of the Imperial Palace}} Within Kyūchū Sanden, in order to oversee the imperial rituals, a separate internal organization distinct from the state administrative body of the [[:en:Imperial Household Agency|Imperial Household Agency]] is established, known as the '''Chōten-shoku''' (掌典職).{{Cite news |title=宮中祭祀|newspaper= |date= |author=宮内庁|url=https://www.kunaicho.go.jp/about/gokomu/kyuchu/saishi/saishi.html|accessdate=2014-10-02}} Under the head of the Chōten, subordinate positions including the Chōten-chō, Chōten, and Naichōten are appointed.{{Sfn|皇室75号|2017|p=43}} The Naichōten (unmarried women serving a role equivalent to miko at ordinary shrines) all reside in the north side of the compound. Every morning from 8:00 AM, the Naichōten in the Ken-sho and Kōrei-den, and the Chōten in the Shin-den, perform the “Nikku no Gi” by offering {{ill|sake|ja|清酒|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/sake|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 日本酒}} and sacred food ([[:en:Shinsen|Shinsen]]). At 8:30 AM, the on-duty chamberlain of the [[:en:Board of Chamberlains|Imperial Household Agency Attendant Office]] conducts the “Maichō Godaihai” on behalf of the emperor in all three halls. These rituals, Nikku no Gi and Maichō Godaihai, are carried out without fail even during periods when the emperor is not in residence ({{ill|Haichō|ja|廃朝|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Haichō|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}) or during periods of imperial mourning. The ceremonial practices of Kyūchū Sanden were established after the Meiji Restoration, through successive reforms and gradual consolidation of imperial rites, and are understood to have been finalized on April 2 (lunar calendar) in the 5th year of Meiji ([[:en:1872|1872]] / May 8) shortly after the establishment of the Ministry of Divinities ([[:en:Ministry of Religion (Japan)|Ministry of Religion]]).{{Cite news |title=維新期「宮中三殿」成立史の一考察―毎朝御拝「石灰壇」祭祀の終焉として―|newspaper=明治聖徳記念学会紀要〔復刊第45号〕|date=2008-11|author=石野浩司|url=http://www.mkc.gr.jp/seitoku/pdf/f45-4.pdf|accessdate=2014-10-02}} At that time, the sandai-den (砂拝殿) within the Imperial Palace was relocated to the Akasaka Temporary Imperial Palace after being damaged by a fire in September of [[:en:1873|1873]] (Meiji 6). The current structures of Kyūchū Sanden were designed by {{ill|Kikosei Kiyokage|ja|木子清敬|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kikosei Kiyokage|qq=|1=Kigo Kiyoyoshi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11518290}}, a first-class craftsman of the former [[:en:Ministry of the Imperial Household|Ministry of the Imperial Household]], completed in October [[:en:1888|1888]] (Meiji 21) and relocated on January 9 [[:en:1889|1889]] (Meiji 22). During World War II in [[:en:1944|1944]] (Showa 19), the structures were temporarily relocated to the Imperial Palace’s air-raid shelter (the Osai-ko, 御斎庫) to avoid air raids, returning after the end of the war in [[:en:1945|1945]] (Showa 20), and in [[:en:2004|2004]] (Heisei 16) on June 18 were once temporarily moved to a provisional hall (the Kari-dono, 仮殿) set several dozen meters away for seismic deterioration inspections (returning on the 27th of the same month). Additionally, several ancillary buildings are located within the compound. To the west is the Shinka-den (神嘉殿), normally an empty hall, but on November 30 each year, the [[:en:Niiname-no-Matsuri|Niinamesai]] is held and on New Year’s Day ({{ill|Gantan|ja|元旦|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gantan|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 元日|1=New Year's Day|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q196627}}) the 【Shihōhai】 is performed in its front garden. Other structures include the Ryōki-den (綾綺殿), where ceremonies such as the ritual changing of attire for the emperor and empress take place; the Tōgū-bin-den (東宮便殿), where the Crown Prince and Crown Princess change attire; the Kagurasha (神楽舎), where kagura is offered; the Sōgakusha (奏楽舎), where gagaku is performed by musicians; the Hidari-akusha (左幄舎) and Migi-akusha (右幄舎), where attendants wait; the Ken-sho main gate (賢所正門) facing the Ken-sho; and the Shinka-mon (新嘉門) facing the Shinka-den. == The Three Halls == === Kashiko-dokoro === {{main|Kashiko-dokoro}} [[File:Yata no Kagami, artist impression.png|thumb|Yata no Kagami (image); actual object is not publicly displayed]] The Ken-sho enshrines the sacred mirror ([[:en:Yata no Kagami|Yata no Kagami]]) and venerates the ancestral deity {{ill|Amaterasu Ōmikami|ja|天照大御神|1=Amaterasu|lt=Amaterasu Ōmikami|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amaterasu Ōmikami|13=User:Immanuelle/Amaterasu|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 天照大神}}.{{Sfn|皇室75号|2017|p=43}} During the Heian period, the Ken-sho was located at the {{ill|Unmei-den|ja|温明殿|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Unmei-den|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, and from the Kamakura period (and subsequently during the Muromachi period) it was situated at the {{ill|Shunkō-den|ja|春興殿|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shunkō-den|qq=|1=Shunkōden|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11513798}}; in earlier times, it was managed by the {{ill|Naishi|ja|内侍|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Naishi|qq=|1=naishi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11393857}}, hence it was also called the “Naishidokoro” (内侍所).{{Cite web|和書|url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E8%B3%A2%E6%89%80-44278|title=賢所|accessdate=2021-01-17|publisher=[[:en:Kotobank|Kotobank]]}} The Chōten and Naichōten serve the sacred functions, protecting the “sacred fire” (which signifies a holy flame) and are subject to strict protocols such as the “Jisei” system to avoid defilement. Ancient imperial rituals ([[:en:Ritual ceremonies of the Imperial Palace|Ceremonies of the Japanese Imperial Palace]]) have long been performed here, and it is at this location that marriage ceremonies ({{ill|Kekkon no Gi|ja|結婚の儀|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kekkon no Gi|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 皇室の儀式|1=Japanese Imperial Rituals|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11581030}}) welcoming former Empress Dowager [[:en:Empress Michiko|Michiko†Jōkōgō_Michiko]], Empress [[:en:Empress Masako|Masako†Kōgō_Masako]], and other imperial consorts have been held. In such ceremonies, when the empress exits the Ken-sho, the marriage is considered to be solemnized. === Kōrei-den === The Kōrei-den enshrines the spirits of successive emperors and other members of the {{ill|Imperial Family|ja|皇族|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imperial Family|qq=|1=Imperial Family of Japan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11581068}}.{{Sfn|皇室75号|2017|p=43}} During the Meiji Restoration, under the Shinbutsu Hanzenrei, reforms in imperial rites were implemented. In 1862 (Meiji 2), the re-established [[:en:Department of Divinities|Department of Divinities]] (later the Ministry of Divinities) built an auxiliary hall and enshrined the spirits of successive emperors in the Shinto style. As a result, the “Kurodo” (黒戸)—which had been used to enshrine emperors in the Buddhist style since the Heian period—was abolished, and the imperial tablets and statues were transferred to {{ill|Reimei-den at Sensō-ji|ja|霊明殿|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Reimei-den at Sensō-ji|qq=|1=Reimeiden|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q109357129}} at [[:en:Sennyū-ji|Senyū-ji]].{{Cite journal|author=石野浩司|year=2015|title=Establishment of “Reimei-den” during the Meiji Period at Senyū-ji—Imperial Rites and Its Connection with Senyū-ji|journal=明治聖徳記念学会起要|volume=復刊第52号|page=}} On September 14, 1871 (Meiji 4), the Ken-sho was relocated within the palace.{{Sfn|皇典講究所|1909|p=18}} After the relocation to the Akasaka Temporary Imperial Palace in 1873 (Meiji 6) due to fire damage, in 1877 (Meiji 10) the spirits of empresses and other imperial family members were enshrined together with those of the emperors.{{Sfn|皇典講究所|1909|p=18}} In 1885 (Meiji 18), even those emperors who had been posthumously awarded a 【尊号】 were also enshrined.{{Sfn|皇典講究所|1909|p=18}} In 1889 (Meiji 22), with the reconstruction of the Imperial Palace, a new building was constructed on the west side of the Ken-sho.{{Sfn|皇典講究所|1909|p=18}} It is customary that the spirits of the emperor and imperial family are enshrined in the Kōrei-den one year after their death.{{Cite web|和書|url=https://www.nikkei.com/article/DGXNZO56020230Q3A610C1CR0000/|title=天皇陛下、寛仁さまの墓所を参拝|accessdate=2013-06-10|publisher=[[:en:The Nikkei|Nikkei]]}} Every year, the Spring Imperial Festival is held on the Vernal Equinox Day and the Autumn Imperial Festival on the Autumnal Equinox Day. Additionally, on January 7 the Shōwa Tennō-sai (Senteisai) is held, and on April 3 the Jimmu Tennō-sai takes place; in certain ceremonial years, the emperor’s memorial rites are conducted at the imperial mausoleum, and the Crown Prince and Crown Princess participate in rites at the Kōrei-den. === Shin-den === It enshrines the eight million kami, namely {{ill|Tenshin and Kunitsugami|ja|天津神・国津神|1=Kami#Amatsukami_and_Kunitsukami|2=ja|3=天津神・国津神|4=zh|5=天津神與國津神|6=ko|7=아마쓰카미·구니쓰카미|lt=Amatsukami and Kunitsukami|lt=Tenshin Chigi|lt_ja=天神地祇|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tenshin and Kunitsugami|qq=|comment=enwiki is a redirect}}, who comprise the myriad deities of Japan. {{Sfn|皇室75号|2017|p=43}} Originally, this facility was dedicated to enshrining the eight gods and was known as {{ill|Yatsugamaden|ja|八神殿|1=Hasshinden|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yatsugamaden|13=User:Immanuelle/Hasshinden|qq=}}. From the medieval period onward it was maintained in the western wing of the [[:en:Department of Divinities|Department of Divinities]], but by the time of [[:en:Emperor Ōgimachi|Emperor Shōchin-machi]], the associated government offices had been lost. {{Sfn|皇典講究所|1909|p=24}} Consequently, the Urabe clan performed ritual offerings at Kaguragaoka in Yoshida Village, Kyoto, establishing it as a sacred site. However, in Tenshō 18 (1590), by imperial authorization, it was designated as acting on behalf of the Jingi-kan, and the sacred object of the eight gods was enshrined within the residence of the {{ill|Hakugawa Hakuō Family|ja|白川伯王家|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hakugawa Hakuō Family|qq=|1=Shirakawa clan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11579697}}. {{Sfn|皇典講究所|1909|p=25}} In the Meiji era, the [[:en:Department of Divinities|Department of Divinities]] constructed a shrine in Tokyo, and the sacred object was enshrined there on December 17, Meiji 2 (1862). {{Sfn|皇典講究所|1909|p=25-26}} After the Jingi-kan was reorganized into the Ministry of Divinities—and that ministry was abolished in Meiji 5 (1872)—the eight gods and {{ill|Tenshin Chigi|ja|天神地祇|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tenshin Chigi|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 天津神・国津神|1=Amatsukami and Kunitsukami|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11442793}} were transferred to the Imperial Court. On November 27 of that same year they were enshrined together and the shrine was renamed as the Shin-den. {{Sfn|皇典講究所|1909|p=26-27}} Every year, on the Vernal Equinox Day and the Autumnal Equinox Day, the spring and autumn Shin-den festivals are held. == Footnotes == {{Reflist}} == References == * {{Citation|和書|author=皇典講究所|title=宮中三殿並に祝祭日解説|publisher=国晃館|year=1909}} * As this translation isn't very good atm[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 08:22, 13 March 2025 (UTC)}} [[File:Three Palace Sanctuaries.jpg|thumb|Three Palace Sanctuaries]] The {{Nihongo|'''Three Palace Sanctuaries'''|宮中三殿|Kyūchū sanden}} are a group of structures in the precincts of the [[Tokyo Imperial Palace]] in [[:en:Japan|Japan]]. They are used in imperial religious ceremonies, including weddings and [[Enthronement of the Japanese emperor|enthronements]]. The three sanctuaries are: * ''Kashiko-dokoro'' (賢所) – the central shrine, enshrining a replica of the mirror [[Yata no Kagami]], representing the mythological ancestress of the [[:en:Imperial Family of Japan|Imperial Family]], [[Amaterasu]]. (For the enthronements in [[:en:Kyoto|Kyoto]] of [[:en:Emperor Taishō|Emperor Taishō]] in 1915 and of [[:en:Emperor Shōwa|Emperor Shōwa]] in 1928, the mirror was transported by special [[:en:Rolling stock|Rolling stock]] known as the ''Kashiko-dokoro Jōgyosha'' (賢所乗御車) from the name of this sanctuary.) The ''[[:en:Yasakani no magatama|Yasakani no magatama]]'' or Sacred Jewel, one of the [[:en:Imperial Regalia of Japan|Imperial Regalia of Japan]], is also said to be housed in the Kashiko-dokoro. * ''Kōrei-den'' (皇霊殿) – the [[:en:Ancestral spirits|Ancestral Spirits]] Sanctuary, enshrining the departed spirits of the Imperial Family from one year after their death. * ''Shin-den'' (神殿) – the Sanctuary of the ''[[Kami]]'', enshrining the ''[[Amatsukami]]'' (天津神) from [[Takamagahara]] and the ''Kunitsukami'' (国津神) from [[Japanese mythology]]. {{infobox Shinto shrine | name = Kyūchū Sanden | image = [[File:Three Palace Sanctuaries.jpg|290px]] | location = {{JPN}}・[[:en:Tokyo|Tokyo Metropolis]]・[[:en:Chiyoda, Tokyo|Chiyoda Ward]]・[[:en:Chiyoda, Chiyoda, Tokyo|Chiyoda]] 1-1 | coordinates = {{coord|35|40|54|N|139|44|59|E|display=inline,title}} | enshrined deities = Ken-sho: {{ill|Amaterasu Ōmikami|ja|天照大御神|1=Amaterasu|lt=Amaterasu Ōmikami|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amaterasu Ōmikami|13=User:Immanuelle/Amaterasu|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 天照大神}}
Kōrei-den: [[:en:List of emperors of Japan|Emperors]]・{{ill|Imperial Family|ja|皇族|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imperial Family|qq=|1=Imperial Family of Japan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11581068}} spirits
Shin-den: {{ill|Tenshin Chigi|ja|天神地祇|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tenshin Chigi|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 天津神・国津神|1=Amatsukami and Kunitsukami|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11442793}} | shrine Rank = None | annual festival = Ken-sho: January 3 ({{ill|Ganshiki-sai|ja|元始祭|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ganshiki-sai|qq=|1=Genshisai|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11387821}}) ・ October 17 ([[:en:Kannamesai Festival|Kannamesai]])

Shinka-den: November 23 ([[:en:Niiname-no-Matsuri|Niinamesai]]) }} '''Kyūchū Sanden''' (宮中三殿【きゅうちゅうさんでん】) is the collective name for the three sanctuaries—the '''Ken-sho''' (賢所), '''Kōrei-den''' (皇霊殿), and '''Shin-den''' (神殿)—located within the [[:en:Tokyo Imperial Palace|Imperial Palace]]’s {{ill|Fukiage Gyoen|ja|吹上御苑|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Fukiage Gyoen|qq=|1=Fukiage Gyoen|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11288366}}. These three halls are also collectively referred to as the “Ken-sho” (賢所, けんしょ).{{Cite book|和書|title=Imperial Household Encyclopedia (Reiwa Edition)|date=2019th year 11月30日|year=2019|publisher={{ill|KADOKAWA|ja|株式会社KADOKAWA|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/KADOKAWA|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to KADOKAWA|1=Kadokawa Corporation|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q17224985}}}} Kyūchū Sanden consists of three parts: at its center is the Ken-sho, which enshrines the imperial ancestral deity {{ill|Amaterasu Ōmikami|ja|天照大御神|1=Amaterasu|lt=Amaterasu Ōmikami|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amaterasu Ōmikami|13=User:Immanuelle/Amaterasu|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 天照大神}}; to its west is the Kōrei-den, which enshrines the spirits of successive emperors {{ill|List of Emperors|ja|歴代の天皇|lt=Emperors|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/List of Emperors|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 天皇の一覧|1=list of Emperors of Japan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q188210}} and empresses as well as other members of the {{ill|Imperial Family|ja|皇族|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imperial Family|qq=|1=Imperial Family of Japan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11581068}}; and to its east is the Shin-den, which enshrines the myriad kami ({{ill|Tenshin Chigi|ja|天神地祇|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tenshin Chigi|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 天津神・国津神|1=Amatsukami and Kunitsukami|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11442793}}) of the Japanese pantheon.{{Sfn|皇室75号|2017|p=43}} == Overview == {{Double image aside|right|Emperor Akihito 199011 1.jpg|290|Emperor Akihito, Daijosai (1990).jpg|172|{{ill|Kōroshūzome Gohō|ja|黄櫨染御袍|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōroshūzome Gohō|qq=|1=Kōrozen no gohō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11677782}} and ceremonial garments worn during the reign of [[:en:Akihito|Akihito]]}} Kyūchū Sanden is constructed facing south, with the Ken-sho centrally located, the Kōrei-den to its west, and the Shin-den to its east.{{Sfn|皇室75号|2017|p=42}} The Ken-sho is the largest among the three. The architecture of Kyūchū Sanden is of a single-story [[:en:East Asian hip-and-gable roof|Irimoya-zukuri]] style with {{ill|Saimoto|ja|妻入|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Saimoto|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 切妻造|1=rake-overhanging gabled roof|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q13308575}}, built of white wood with decorative elements on the front and back.{{Sfn|皇室75号|2017|p=42}} Originally, the roofs were clad in {{ill|Hinoki bark|ja|檜皮葺|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hinoki bark|qq=|1=cypress bark roof|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q90373477}}, but were later replaced with copper plates.{{Cite book|title=Shirarezaru Kōshitsu – From Traditional Ceremonies to the Work of the Imperial Household Agency|date=2010th year 1月30日|year=2010|publisher=[[:en:Kawade Shobō Shinsha|Kawade Shobo Shinsha]]}} The interiors of the three halls are divided into the outer court, inner court, and innermost court (naichinai-den).{{Sfn|皇室75号|2017|p=42}} The buildings feature wooden floors, with sliding doors such as half-fusuma (【半蔀】, hajitomi) and shōji, and are surrounded by lattice work ({{ill|Sudare|ja|簀子|lt=Sudare|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sudare|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to すのこ|1=duckboards|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q2933208}}). In front, each has wooden steps, further preceded by stone steps.{{Sfn|皇室75号|2017|p=42}} == Rituals and Ceremonies == {{seealso|Ritual ceremonies of the Imperial Palace}} Within Kyūchū Sanden, in order to oversee the imperial rituals, a separate internal organization distinct from the state administrative body of the [[:en:Imperial Household Agency|Imperial Household Agency]] is established, known as the '''Chōten-shoku''' (掌典職).{{Cite news |title=宮中祭祀|newspaper= |date= |author=宮内庁|url=https://www.kunaicho.go.jp/about/gokomu/kyuchu/saishi/saishi.html|accessdate=2014-10-02}} Under the head of the Chōten, subordinate positions including the Chōten-chō, Chōten, and Naichōten are appointed.{{Sfn|皇室75号|2017|p=43}} The Naichōten (unmarried women serving a role equivalent to miko at ordinary shrines) all reside in the north side of the compound. Every morning from 8:00 AM, the Naichōten in the Ken-sho and Kōrei-den, and the Chōten in the Shin-den, perform the “Nikku no Gi” by offering {{ill|sake|ja|清酒|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/sake|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 日本酒}} and sacred food ([[:en:Shinsen|Shinsen]]). At 8:30 AM, the on-duty chamberlain of the [[:en:Board of Chamberlains|Imperial Household Agency Attendant Office]] conducts the “Maichō Godaihai” on behalf of the emperor in all three halls. These rituals, Nikku no Gi and Maichō Godaihai, are carried out without fail even during periods when the emperor is not in residence ({{ill|Haichō|ja|廃朝|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Haichō|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}) or during periods of imperial mourning. The ceremonial practices of Kyūchū Sanden were established after the Meiji Restoration, through successive reforms and gradual consolidation of imperial rites, and are understood to have been finalized on April 2 (lunar calendar) in the 5th year of Meiji ([[:en:1872|1872]] / May 8) shortly after the establishment of the Ministry of Divinities ([[:en:Ministry of Religion (Japan)|Ministry of Religion]]).{{Cite news |title=維新期「宮中三殿」成立史の一考察―毎朝御拝「石灰壇」祭祀の終焉として―|newspaper=明治聖徳記念学会紀要〔復刊第45号〕|date=2008-11|author=石野浩司|url=http://www.mkc.gr.jp/seitoku/pdf/f45-4.pdf|accessdate=2014-10-02}} At that time, the sandai-den (砂拝殿) within the Imperial Palace was relocated to the Akasaka Temporary Imperial Palace after being damaged by a fire in September of [[:en:1873|1873]] (Meiji 6). The current structures of Kyūchū Sanden were designed by {{ill|Kikosei Kiyokage|ja|木子清敬|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kikosei Kiyokage|qq=|1=Kigo Kiyoyoshi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11518290}}, a first-class craftsman of the former [[:en:Ministry of the Imperial Household|Ministry of the Imperial Household]], completed in October [[:en:1888|1888]] (Meiji 21) and relocated on January 9 [[:en:1889|1889]] (Meiji 22). During World War II in [[:en:1944|1944]] (Showa 19), the structures were temporarily relocated to the Imperial Palace’s air-raid shelter (the Osai-ko, 御斎庫) to avoid air raids, returning after the end of the war in [[:en:1945|1945]] (Showa 20), and in [[:en:2004|2004]] (Heisei 16) on June 18 were once temporarily moved to a provisional hall (the Kari-dono, 仮殿) set several dozen meters away for seismic deterioration inspections (returning on the 27th of the same month). Additionally, several ancillary buildings are located within the compound. To the west is the Shinka-den (神嘉殿), normally an empty hall, but on November 30 each year, the [[:en:Niiname-no-Matsuri|Niinamesai]] is held and on New Year’s Day ({{ill|Gantan|ja|元旦|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gantan|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 元日|1=New Year's Day|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q196627}}) the 【Shihōhai】 is performed in its front garden. Other structures include the Ryōki-den (綾綺殿), where ceremonies such as the ritual changing of attire for the emperor and empress take place; the Tōgū-bin-den (東宮便殿), where the Crown Prince and Crown Princess change attire; the Kagurasha (神楽舎), where kagura is offered; the Sōgakusha (奏楽舎), where gagaku is performed by musicians; the Hidari-akusha (左幄舎) and Migi-akusha (右幄舎), where attendants wait; the Ken-sho main gate (賢所正門) facing the Ken-sho; and the Shinka-mon (新嘉門) facing the Shinka-den. == The Three Halls == === Kashiko-dokoro === {{main|Kashiko-dokoro}} [[File:Yata no Kagami, artist impression.png|thumb|Yata no Kagami (image); actual object is not publicly displayed]] The Ken-sho enshrines the sacred mirror ([[:en:Yata no Kagami|Yata no Kagami]]) and venerates the ancestral deity {{ill|Amaterasu Ōmikami|ja|天照大御神|1=Amaterasu|lt=Amaterasu Ōmikami|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amaterasu Ōmikami|13=User:Immanuelle/Amaterasu|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 天照大神}}.{{Sfn|皇室75号|2017|p=43}} During the Heian period, the Ken-sho was located at the {{ill|Unmei-den|ja|温明殿|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Unmei-den|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, and from the Kamakura period (and subsequently during the Muromachi period) it was situated at the {{ill|Shunkō-den|ja|春興殿|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shunkō-den|qq=|1=Shunkōden|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11513798}}; in earlier times, it was managed by the {{ill|Naishi|ja|内侍|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Naishi|qq=|1=naishi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11393857}}, hence it was also called the “Naishidokoro” (内侍所).{{Cite web|和書|url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E8%B3%A2%E6%89%80-44278|title=賢所|accessdate=2021-01-17|publisher=[[:en:Kotobank|Kotobank]]}} The Chōten and Naichōten serve the sacred functions, protecting the “sacred fire” (which signifies a holy flame) and are subject to strict protocols such as the “Jisei” system to avoid defilement. Ancient imperial rituals ([[:en:Ritual ceremonies of the Imperial Palace|Ceremonies of the Japanese Imperial Palace]]) have long been performed here, and it is at this location that marriage ceremonies ({{ill|Kekkon no Gi|ja|結婚の儀|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kekkon no Gi|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 皇室の儀式|1=Japanese Imperial Rituals|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11581030}}) welcoming former Empress Dowager [[:en:Empress Michiko|Michiko†Jōkōgō_Michiko]], Empress [[:en:Empress Masako|Masako†Kōgō_Masako]], and other imperial consorts have been held. In such ceremonies, when the empress exits the Ken-sho, the marriage is considered to be solemnized. === Kōrei-den === The Kōrei-den enshrines the spirits of successive emperors and other members of the {{ill|Imperial Family|ja|皇族|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imperial Family|qq=|1=Imperial Family of Japan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11581068}}.{{Sfn|皇室75号|2017|p=43}} During the Meiji Restoration, under the Shinbutsu Hanzenrei, reforms in imperial rites were implemented. In 1862 (Meiji 2), the re-established [[:en:Department of Divinities|Department of Divinities]] (later the Ministry of Divinities) built an auxiliary hall and enshrined the spirits of successive emperors in the Shinto style. As a result, the “Kurodo” (黒戸)—which had been used to enshrine emperors in the Buddhist style since the Heian period—was abolished, and the imperial tablets and statues were transferred to {{ill|Reimei-den at Sensō-ji|ja|霊明殿|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Reimei-den at Sensō-ji|qq=|1=Reimeiden|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q109357129}} at [[:en:Sennyū-ji|Senyū-ji]].{{Cite journal|author=石野浩司|year=2015|title=Establishment of “Reimei-den” during the Meiji Period at Senyū-ji—Imperial Rites and Its Connection with Senyū-ji|journal=明治聖徳記念学会起要|volume=復刊第52号|page=}} On September 14, 1871 (Meiji 4), the Ken-sho was relocated within the palace.{{Sfn|皇典講究所|1909|p=18}} After the relocation to the Akasaka Temporary Imperial Palace in 1873 (Meiji 6) due to fire damage, in 1877 (Meiji 10) the spirits of empresses and other imperial family members were enshrined together with those of the emperors.{{Sfn|皇典講究所|1909|p=18}} In 1885 (Meiji 18), even those emperors who had been posthumously awarded a 【尊号】 were also enshrined.{{Sfn|皇典講究所|1909|p=18}} In 1889 (Meiji 22), with the reconstruction of the Imperial Palace, a new building was constructed on the west side of the Ken-sho.{{Sfn|皇典講究所|1909|p=18}} It is customary that the spirits of the emperor and imperial family are enshrined in the Kōrei-den one year after their death.{{Cite web|和書|url=https://www.nikkei.com/article/DGXNZO56020230Q3A610C1CR0000/|title=天皇陛下、寛仁さまの墓所を参拝|accessdate=2013-06-10|publisher=[[:en:The Nikkei|Nikkei]]}} Every year, the Spring Imperial Festival is held on the Vernal Equinox Day and the Autumn Imperial Festival on the Autumnal Equinox Day. Additionally, on January 7 the Shōwa Tennō-sai (Senteisai) is held, and on April 3 the Jimmu Tennō-sai takes place; in certain ceremonial years, the emperor’s memorial rites are conducted at the imperial mausoleum, and the Crown Prince and Crown Princess participate in rites at the Kōrei-den. === Shin-den === It enshrines the eight million kami, namely {{ill|Tenshin and Kunitsugami|ja|天津神・国津神|1=Kami#Amatsukami_and_Kunitsukami|2=ja|3=天津神・国津神|4=zh|5=天津神與國津神|6=ko|7=아마쓰카미·구니쓰카미|lt=Amatsukami and Kunitsukami|lt=Tenshin Chigi|lt_ja=天神地祇|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tenshin and Kunitsugami|qq=|comment=enwiki is a redirect}}, who comprise the myriad deities of Japan. {{Sfn|皇室75号|2017|p=43}} Originally, this facility was dedicated to enshrining the eight gods and was known as {{ill|Yatsugamaden|ja|八神殿|1=Hasshinden|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yatsugamaden|13=User:Immanuelle/Hasshinden|qq=}}. From the medieval period onward it was maintained in the western wing of the [[:en:Department of Divinities|Department of Divinities]], but by the time of [[:en:Emperor Ōgimachi|Emperor Shōchin-machi]], the associated government offices had been lost. {{Sfn|皇典講究所|1909|p=24}} Consequently, the Urabe clan performed ritual offerings at Kaguragaoka in Yoshida Village, Kyoto, establishing it as a sacred site. However, in Tenshō 18 (1590), by imperial authorization, it was designated as acting on behalf of the Jingi-kan, and the sacred object of the eight gods was enshrined within the residence of the {{ill|Hakugawa Hakuō Family|ja|白川伯王家|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hakugawa Hakuō Family|qq=|1=Shirakawa clan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11579697}}. {{Sfn|皇典講究所|1909|p=25}} In the Meiji era, the [[:en:Department of Divinities|Department of Divinities]] constructed a shrine in Tokyo, and the sacred object was enshrined there on December 17, Meiji 2 (1862). {{Sfn|皇典講究所|1909|p=25-26}} After the Jingi-kan was reorganized into the Ministry of Divinities—and that ministry was abolished in Meiji 5 (1872)—the eight gods and {{ill|Tenshin Chigi|ja|天神地祇|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tenshin Chigi|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 天津神・国津神|1=Amatsukami and Kunitsukami|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11442793}} were transferred to the Imperial Court. On November 27 of that same year they were enshrined together and the shrine was renamed as the Shin-den. {{Sfn|皇典講究所|1909|p=26-27}} Every year, on the Vernal Equinox Day and the Autumnal Equinox Day, the spring and autumn Shin-den festivals are held. == Footnotes == {{Reflist}} == References == * {{Citation|和書|author=皇典講究所|title=宮中三殿並に祝祭日解説|publisher=国晃館|year=1909}} * As this translation isn't very good atm[[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 08:22, 13 March 2025 (UTC)}} [[File:Three Palace Sanctuaries.jpg|thumb|Three Palace Sanctuaries]] The {{Nihongo|'''Three Palace Sanctuaries'''|宮中三殿|Kyūchū sanden}} are a group of structures in the precincts of the [[Tokyo Imperial Palace]] in [[:en:Japan|Japan]]. They are used in imperial religious ceremonies, including weddings and [[Enthronement of the Japanese emperor|enthronements]]. The three sanctuaries are: * ''Kashiko-dokoro'' (賢所) – the central shrine, enshrining a replica of the mirror [[Yata no Kagami]], representing the mythological ancestress of the [[:en:Imperial Family of Japan|Imperial Family]], [[Amaterasu]]. (For the enthronements in [[:en:Kyoto|Kyoto]] of [[:en:Emperor Taishō|Emperor Taishō]] in 1915 and of [[:en:Emperor Shōwa|Emperor Shōwa]] in 1928, the mirror was transported by special [[:en:Rolling stock|Rolling stock]] known as the ''Kashiko-dokoro Jōgyosha'' (賢所乗御車) from the name of this sanctuary.) The ''[[:en:Yasakani no magatama|Yasakani no magatama]]'' or Sacred Jewel, one of the [[:en:Imperial Regalia of Japan|Imperial Regalia of Japan]], is also said to be housed in the Kashiko-dokoro. * ''Kōrei-den'' (皇霊殿) – the [[:en:Ancestral spirits|Ancestral Spirits]] Sanctuary, enshrining the departed spirits of the Imperial Family from one year after their death. * ''Shin-den'' (神殿) – the Sanctuary of the ''[[Kami]]'', enshrining the ''[[Amatsukami]]'' (天津神) from [[Takamagahara]] and the ''Kunitsukami'' (国津神) from [[Japanese mythology]]. {{infobox Shinto shrine | name = Kyūchū Sanden | image = [[File:Three Palace Sanctuaries.jpg|290px]] | location = {{JPN}}・[[:en:Tokyo|Tokyo Metropolis]]・[[:en:Chiyoda, Tokyo|Chiyoda Ward]]・[[:en:Chiyoda, Chiyoda, Tokyo|Chiyoda]] 1-1 | coordinates = {{coord|35|40|54|N|139|44|59|E|display=inline,title}} | enshrined deities = Ken-sho: {{ill|Amaterasu Ōmikami|ja|天照大御神|1=Amaterasu|lt=Amaterasu Ōmikami|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amaterasu Ōmikami|13=User:Immanuelle/Amaterasu|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 天照大神}}
Kōrei-den: [[:en:List of emperors of Japan|Emperors]]・{{ill|Imperial Family|ja|皇族|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imperial Family|qq=|1=Imperial Family of Japan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11581068}} spirits
Shin-den: {{ill|Tenshin Chigi|ja|天神地祇|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tenshin Chigi|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 天津神・国津神|1=Amatsukami and Kunitsukami|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11442793}} | shrine Rank = None | annual festival = Ken-sho: January 3 ({{ill|Ganshiki-sai|ja|元始祭|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ganshiki-sai|qq=|1=Genshisai|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11387821}}) ・ October 17 ([[:en:Kannamesai Festival|Kannamesai]])
Kōrei-den: January 7 ({{ill|Senteisai|ja|先帝祭|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Senteisai|qq=|1=Previous Emperor Festival|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11388139}}) ・ {{ill|Vernal Equinox Day|ja|春分日|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Vernal Equinox Day|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 春分|1=Chunfen|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1339268}} ({{ill|Spring Imperial Festival|ja|春季皇霊祭|1=Kōreisai|lt=Spring Kōreisai|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Spring Imperial Festival|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōreisai|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 皇霊祭}}) ・ April 3 ({{ill|Jimmu Tennō-sai|ja|神武天皇祭|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Jimmu Tennō-sai|qq=|1=Emperor Jinmu Festival|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11590440}}) ・ {{ill|Autumnal Equinox Day|ja|秋分日|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Autumnal Equinox Day|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 秋分|1=Qiufen|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1200436}} (Autumn Imperial Festival)
Shin-den: Vernal Equinox Day (Spring Shrine Festival) ・ Autumnal Equinox Day (Autumn Shrine Festival)
Shinka-den: November 23 ([[:en:Niiname-no-Matsuri|Niinamesai]]) }} '''Kyūchū Sanden''' (宮中三殿【きゅうちゅうさんでん】) is the collective name for the three sanctuaries—the '''Ken-sho''' (賢所), '''Kōrei-den''' (皇霊殿), and '''Shin-den''' (神殿)—located within the [[:en:Tokyo Imperial Palace|Imperial Palace]]’s {{ill|Fukiage Gyoen|ja|吹上御苑|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Fukiage Gyoen|qq=|1=Fukiage Gyoen|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11288366}}. These three halls are also collectively referred to as the “Ken-sho” (賢所, けんしょ).{{Cite book|和書|title=Imperial Household Encyclopedia (Reiwa Edition)|date=2019th year 11月30日|year=2019|publisher={{ill|KADOKAWA|ja|株式会社KADOKAWA|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/KADOKAWA|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to KADOKAWA|1=Kadokawa Corporation|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q17224985}}}} Kyūchū Sanden consists of three parts: at its center is the Ken-sho, which enshrines the imperial ancestral deity {{ill|Amaterasu Ōmikami|ja|天照大御神|1=Amaterasu|lt=Amaterasu Ōmikami|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amaterasu Ōmikami|13=User:Immanuelle/Amaterasu|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 天照大神}}; to its west is the Kōrei-den, which enshrines the spirits of successive emperors {{ill|List of Emperors|ja|歴代の天皇|lt=Emperors|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/List of Emperors|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 天皇の一覧|1=list of Emperors of Japan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q188210}} and empresses as well as other members of the {{ill|Imperial Family|ja|皇族|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imperial Family|qq=|1=Imperial Family of Japan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11581068}}; and to its east is the Shin-den, which enshrines the myriad kami ({{ill|Tenshin Chigi|ja|天神地祇|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tenshin Chigi|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 天津神・国津神|1=Amatsukami and Kunitsukami|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11442793}}) of the Japanese pantheon.{{Sfn|皇室75号|2017|p=43}} == Overview == {{Double image aside|right|Emperor Akihito 199011 1.jpg|290|Emperor Akihito, Daijosai (1990).jpg|172|{{ill|Kōroshūzome Gohō|ja|黄櫨染御袍|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kōroshūzome Gohō|qq=|1=Kōrozen no gohō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11677782}} and ceremonial garments worn during the reign of [[:en:Akihito|Akihito]]}} Kyūchū Sanden is constructed facing south, with the Ken-sho centrally located, the Kōrei-den to its west, and the Shin-den to its east.{{Sfn|皇室75号|2017|p=42}} The Ken-sho is the largest among the three. The architecture of Kyūchū Sanden is of a single-story [[:en:East Asian hip-and-gable roof|Irimoya-zukuri]] style with {{ill|Saimoto|ja|妻入|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Saimoto|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 切妻造|1=rake-overhanging gabled roof|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q13308575}}, built of white wood with decorative elements on the front and back.{{Sfn|皇室75号|2017|p=42}} Originally, the roofs were clad in {{ill|Hinoki bark|ja|檜皮葺|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hinoki bark|qq=|1=cypress bark roof|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q90373477}}, but were later replaced with copper plates.{{Cite book|title=Shirarezaru Kōshitsu – From Traditional Ceremonies to the Work of the Imperial Household Agency|date=2010th year 1月30日|year=2010|publisher=[[:en:Kawade Shobō Shinsha|Kawade Shobo Shinsha]]}} The interiors of the three halls are divided into the outer court, inner court, and innermost court (naichinai-den).{{Sfn|皇室75号|2017|p=42}} The buildings feature wooden floors, with sliding doors such as half-fusuma (【半蔀】, hajitomi) and shōji, and are surrounded by lattice work ({{ill|Sudare|ja|簀子|lt=Sudare|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sudare|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to すのこ|1=duckboards|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q2933208}}). In front, each has wooden steps, further preceded by stone steps.{{Sfn|皇室75号|2017|p=42}} == Rituals and Ceremonies == {{seealso|Ritual ceremonies of the Imperial Palace}} Within Kyūchū Sanden, in order to oversee the imperial rituals, a separate internal organization distinct from the state administrative body of the [[:en:Imperial Household Agency|Imperial Household Agency]] is established, known as the '''Chōten-shoku''' (掌典職).{{Cite news |title=宮中祭祀|newspaper= |date= |author=宮内庁|url=https://www.kunaicho.go.jp/about/gokomu/kyuchu/saishi/saishi.html|accessdate=2014-10-02}} Under the head of the Chōten, subordinate positions including the Chōten-chō, Chōten, and Naichōten are appointed.{{Sfn|皇室75号|2017|p=43}} The Naichōten (unmarried women serving a role equivalent to miko at ordinary shrines) all reside in the north side of the compound. Every morning from 8:00 AM, the Naichōten in the Ken-sho and Kōrei-den, and the Chōten in the Shin-den, perform the “Nikku no Gi” by offering {{ill|sake|ja|清酒|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/sake|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 日本酒}} and sacred food ([[:en:Shinsen|Shinsen]]). At 8:30 AM, the on-duty chamberlain of the [[:en:Board of Chamberlains|Imperial Household Agency Attendant Office]] conducts the “Maichō Godaihai” on behalf of the emperor in all three halls. These rituals, Nikku no Gi and Maichō Godaihai, are carried out without fail even during periods when the emperor is not in residence ({{ill|Haichō|ja|廃朝|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Haichō|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}) or during periods of imperial mourning. The ceremonial practices of Kyūchū Sanden were established after the Meiji Restoration, through successive reforms and gradual consolidation of imperial rites, and are understood to have been finalized on April 2 (lunar calendar) in the 5th year of Meiji ([[:en:1872|1872]] / May 8) shortly after the establishment of the Ministry of Divinities ([[:en:Ministry of Religion (Japan)|Ministry of Religion]]).{{Cite news |title=維新期「宮中三殿」成立史の一考察―毎朝御拝「石灰壇」祭祀の終焉として―|newspaper=明治聖徳記念学会紀要〔復刊第45号〕|date=2008-11|author=石野浩司|url=http://www.mkc.gr.jp/seitoku/pdf/f45-4.pdf|accessdate=2014-10-02}} At that time, the sandai-den (砂拝殿) within the Imperial Palace was relocated to the Akasaka Temporary Imperial Palace after being damaged by a fire in September of [[:en:1873|1873]] (Meiji 6). The current structures of Kyūchū Sanden were designed by {{ill|Kikosei Kiyokage|ja|木子清敬|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kikosei Kiyokage|qq=|1=Kigo Kiyoyoshi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11518290}}, a first-class craftsman of the former [[:en:Ministry of the Imperial Household|Ministry of the Imperial Household]], completed in October [[:en:1888|1888]] (Meiji 21) and relocated on January 9 [[:en:1889|1889]] (Meiji 22). During World War II in [[:en:1944|1944]] (Showa 19), the structures were temporarily relocated to the Imperial Palace’s air-raid shelter (the Osai-ko, 御斎庫) to avoid air raids, returning after the end of the war in [[:en:1945|1945]] (Showa 20), and in [[:en:2004|2004]] (Heisei 16) on June 18 were once temporarily moved to a provisional hall (the Kari-dono, 仮殿) set several dozen meters away for seismic deterioration inspections (returning on the 27th of the same month). Additionally, several ancillary buildings are located within the compound. To the west is the Shinka-den (神嘉殿), normally an empty hall, but on November 30 each year, the [[:en:Niiname-no-Matsuri|Niinamesai]] is held and on New Year’s Day ({{ill|Gantan|ja|元旦|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Gantan|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 元日|1=New Year's Day|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q196627}}) the 【Shihōhai】 is performed in its front garden. Other structures include the Ryōki-den (綾綺殿), where ceremonies such as the ritual changing of attire for the emperor and empress take place; the Tōgū-bin-den (東宮便殿), where the Crown Prince and Crown Princess change attire; the Kagurasha (神楽舎), where kagura is offered; the Sōgakusha (奏楽舎), where gagaku is performed by musicians; the Hidari-akusha (左幄舎) and Migi-akusha (右幄舎), where attendants wait; the Ken-sho main gate (賢所正門) facing the Ken-sho; and the Shinka-mon (新嘉門) facing the Shinka-den. == The Three Halls == === Kashiko-dokoro === {{main|Kashiko-dokoro}} [[File:Yata no Kagami, artist impression.png|thumb|Yata no Kagami (image); actual object is not publicly displayed]] The Ken-sho enshrines the sacred mirror ([[:en:Yata no Kagami|Yata no Kagami]]) and venerates the ancestral deity {{ill|Amaterasu Ōmikami|ja|天照大御神|1=Amaterasu|lt=Amaterasu Ōmikami|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Amaterasu Ōmikami|13=User:Immanuelle/Amaterasu|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 天照大神}}.{{Sfn|皇室75号|2017|p=43}} During the Heian period, the Ken-sho was located at the {{ill|Unmei-den|ja|温明殿|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Unmei-den|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, and from the Kamakura period (and subsequently during the Muromachi period) it was situated at the {{ill|Shunkō-den|ja|春興殿|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shunkō-den|qq=|1=Shunkōden|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11513798}}; in earlier times, it was managed by the {{ill|Naishi|ja|内侍|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Naishi|qq=|1=naishi|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11393857}}, hence it was also called the “Naishidokoro” (内侍所).{{Cite web|和書|url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E8%B3%A2%E6%89%80-44278|title=賢所|accessdate=2021-01-17|publisher=[[:en:Kotobank|Kotobank]]}} The Chōten and Naichōten serve the sacred functions, protecting the “sacred fire” (which signifies a holy flame) and are subject to strict protocols such as the “Jisei” system to avoid defilement. Ancient imperial rituals ([[:en:Ritual ceremonies of the Imperial Palace|Ceremonies of the Japanese Imperial Palace]]) have long been performed here, and it is at this location that marriage ceremonies ({{ill|Kekkon no Gi|ja|結婚の儀|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kekkon no Gi|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 皇室の儀式|1=Japanese Imperial Rituals|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11581030}}) welcoming former Empress Dowager [[:en:Empress Michiko|Michiko†Jōkōgō_Michiko]], Empress [[:en:Empress Masako|Masako†Kōgō_Masako]], and other imperial consorts have been held. In such ceremonies, when the empress exits the Ken-sho, the marriage is considered to be solemnized. === Kōrei-den === The Kōrei-den enshrines the spirits of successive emperors and other members of the {{ill|Imperial Family|ja|皇族|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imperial Family|qq=|1=Imperial Family of Japan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11581068}}.{{Sfn|皇室75号|2017|p=43}} During the Meiji Restoration, under the Shinbutsu Hanzenrei, reforms in imperial rites were implemented. In 1862 (Meiji 2), the re-established [[:en:Department of Divinities|Department of Divinities]] (later the Ministry of Divinities) built an auxiliary hall and enshrined the spirits of successive emperors in the Shinto style. As a result, the “Kurodo” (黒戸)—which had been used to enshrine emperors in the Buddhist style since the Heian period—was abolished, and the imperial tablets and statues were transferred to {{ill|Reimei-den at Sensō-ji|ja|霊明殿|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Reimei-den at Sensō-ji|qq=|1=Reimeiden|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q109357129}} at [[:en:Sennyū-ji|Senyū-ji]].{{Cite journal|author=石野浩司|year=2015|title=Establishment of “Reimei-den” during the Meiji Period at Senyū-ji—Imperial Rites and Its Connection with Senyū-ji|journal=明治聖徳記念学会起要|volume=復刊第52号|page=}} On September 14, 1871 (Meiji 4), the Ken-sho was relocated within the palace.{{Sfn|皇典講究所|1909|p=18}} After the relocation to the Akasaka Temporary Imperial Palace in 1873 (Meiji 6) due to fire damage, in 1877 (Meiji 10) the spirits of empresses and other imperial family members were enshrined together with those of the emperors.{{Sfn|皇典講究所|1909|p=18}} In 1885 (Meiji 18), even those emperors who had been posthumously awarded a 【尊号】 were also enshrined.{{Sfn|皇典講究所|1909|p=18}} In 1889 (Meiji 22), with the reconstruction of the Imperial Palace, a new building was constructed on the west side of the Ken-sho.{{Sfn|皇典講究所|1909|p=18}} It is customary that the spirits of the emperor and imperial family are enshrined in the Kōrei-den one year after their death.{{Cite web|和書|url=https://www.nikkei.com/article/DGXNZO56020230Q3A610C1CR0000/|title=天皇陛下、寛仁さまの墓所を参拝|accessdate=2013-06-10|publisher=[[:en:The Nikkei|Nikkei]]}} Every year, the Spring Imperial Festival is held on the Vernal Equinox Day and the Autumn Imperial Festival on the Autumnal Equinox Day. Additionally, on January 7 the Shōwa Tennō-sai (Senteisai) is held, and on April 3 the Jimmu Tennō-sai takes place; in certain ceremonial years, the emperor’s memorial rites are conducted at the imperial mausoleum, and the Crown Prince and Crown Princess participate in rites at the Kōrei-den. === Shin-den === It enshrines the eight million kami, namely {{ill|Tenshin and Kunitsugami|ja|天津神・国津神|1=Kami#Amatsukami_and_Kunitsukami|2=ja|3=天津神・国津神|4=zh|5=天津神與國津神|6=ko|7=아마쓰카미·구니쓰카미|lt=Amatsukami and Kunitsukami|lt=Tenshin Chigi|lt_ja=天神地祇|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tenshin and Kunitsugami|qq=|comment=enwiki is a redirect}}, who comprise the myriad deities of Japan. {{Sfn|皇室75号|2017|p=43}} Originally, this facility was dedicated to enshrining the eight gods and was known as {{ill|Yatsugamaden|ja|八神殿|1=Hasshinden|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yatsugamaden|13=User:Immanuelle/Hasshinden|qq=}}. From the medieval period onward it was maintained in the western wing of the [[:en:Department of Divinities|Department of Divinities]], but by the time of [[:en:Emperor Ōgimachi|Emperor Shōchin-machi]], the associated government offices had been lost. {{Sfn|皇典講究所|1909|p=24}} Consequently, the Urabe clan performed ritual offerings at Kaguragaoka in Yoshida Village, Kyoto, establishing it as a sacred site. However, in Tenshō 18 (1590), by imperial authorization, it was designated as acting on behalf of the Jingi-kan, and the sacred object of the eight gods was enshrined within the residence of the {{ill|Hakugawa Hakuō Family|ja|白川伯王家|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Hakugawa Hakuō Family|qq=|1=Shirakawa clan|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11579697}}. {{Sfn|皇典講究所|1909|p=25}} In the Meiji era, the [[:en:Department of Divinities|Department of Divinities]] constructed a shrine in Tokyo, and the sacred object was enshrined there on December 17, Meiji 2 (1862). {{Sfn|皇典講究所|1909|p=25-26}} After the Jingi-kan was reorganized into the Ministry of Divinities—and that ministry was abolished in Meiji 5 (1872)—the eight gods and {{ill|Tenshin Chigi|ja|天神地祇|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tenshin Chigi|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 天津神・国津神|1=Amatsukami and Kunitsukami|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11442793}} were transferred to the Imperial Court. On November 27 of that same year they were enshrined together and the shrine was renamed as the Shin-den. {{Sfn|皇典講究所|1909|p=26-27}} Every year, on the Vernal Equinox Day and the Autumnal Equinox Day, the spring and autumn Shin-den festivals are held. == Footnotes == {{Reflist}} == References == * {{Citation|和書|author=皇典講究所|title=宮中三殿並に祝祭日解説|publisher=国晃館|year=1909}} *
